subject: Pecos: workload synthesis & throughput headroom proposal
messages:
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
To: Susan Harper <susan@pecoshealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 5 Jun 2028 09:12:00 -07:00
Subject: Pecos: workload synthesis & throughput headroom proposal

Hi Susan —

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. I pulled together an initial workload synthesis and a lightweight sizing estimate to align on committed capacity for the Pecos pilot / initial launch. The attached CSV and Excel have the raw samples and the math, but key points below so we can move quickly: 

Summary (top-line)
- Model: open-llm-3b (float32 baseline) with q4_0 variant available for Dedicated.
- Observed median request tokens: ~430 tokens; 95th percentile token length from sample: ~1,200 tokens.
- Expected steady-state concurrency (per your note): 60 active reqs, peak concurrency 120 during 15-30 minute spikes.
- Pecos SLO: p95 response latency target <= 400ms for generator-only paths.

Sizing heuristics / estimates (rough)
- Baseline tokens/sec per A100-80GB slab (mixed batching, KV warm): ~14k tps (float32).
- q4_0 quantized variant approximates 1.9x throughput improvement -> ~27k tps per slab.
- Tail-latency & cold-KV warming buffer: allocate safety factor 1.6x for spikes + cache churn.

Initial proposal
- Commit: 8 slabs (A100-80GB equivalent) with q4_0 model variant for Dedicated start.
  - Effective committed throughput (after safety factor): ~27k * 8 / 1.6 ≈ 135k tps capacity headroom.
  - Mapped to your workload: average request ~600 tokens (includes system/context) -> supports ~225 reqs/sec sustained peak.

Questions I need from you to finalize numbers
1) Confirm average tokens per request you expect in production (we used 600 for sizing).
2) Confirm whether the p95 SLO of 400ms is strict for all endpoints or only for the generator path.
3) Procurement timing / constrained start date for Reserved capacity.

Next steps
- If the numbers above look reasonable, Ben and I will prepare a formal commit proposal and an A/B canary plan for the private pilot (10% traffic canary + auto-fallback to hosted variant).

Attachments: pecos_workload_snapshot.csv, initial_sizing_estimate.xlsx

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick call if easier to run through assumptions.

On Tue, Jun 5, 2028 at 09:12, Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com> wrote:
> Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. I pulled together an initial workload synthesis and a lightweight sizing estimate to align on committed capacity for the Pecos pilot / initial launch.

Jordan — this is great, very helpful. Quick clarifications below: 

- Average tokens per request in production: roughly 800 tokens (we have a mix of long summary requests and short probes; median is lower but mean is ~800).
- SLO: p95 <= 400ms is our hard requirement for any synchronous user-facing generator endpoint. Non-critical background jobs can be relaxed.
- Peak concurrency confirmation: yes, concurrent active sessions can hit ~120 for short windows (15–25 minutes).
- Procurement: target to finalize contract by 30 Jun; we can start pilot earlier if we have a committed early-access window.

I attached a small dump of representative ML requests (pecos_mlh_samples.jsonl) — should help tighten token distribution.

Thanks,
Susan Harper
VP of AI, Pecos Health
susan@pecoshealth.com

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 6 Jun 2028 01:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Pecos: workload synthesis & throughput headroom proposal (internal notes)

Jordan / Marissa — digging into Jordan's spreadsheet and Susan's sample set. A few engineering notes and a recommended conservative mapping: 

- Baseline instrumentation: with our continuous-batching runtime and KV prefix-caching, a practical per-slab steady throughput for Pecos (mix of 400–1,200 token requests) is ~16k tps in float32. Quantization to q4_0 moves that to ~30k tps in our test harness for similar sequences. 
- Latency impact: at high concurrency the p95 inflates more than median; recommend we budget 1.6x for tail events (as Jordan suggested) *plus* an extra 10% buffer for cache cold-starts during deploys -> combined safety factor ~1.76x.
- Proposed committed slab math:
  - q4_0 slab effective: 30k tps / 1.76 ≈ 17k usable tps
  - With Susan's 800-token mean -> 21 reqs/sec per slab usable at p95 target
  - To cover 120 peak concurrency sustained (21 reqs/sec * average request duration) and expected spike profile, I recommend an initial commit of 10 slabs (not 8). This gives ~170k usable tps headroom and smoother room for rollouts.

Trade-offs / notes:
- 10 slabs increases monthly committed cost vs 8 (we should model delta in proposal).
- We can offer an initial 90-day phased commit: start at 8 slabs for pilot, auto-scale to 10 slabs on go-live if traffic patterns match samples — include a 2-week measurement window.

I'll drop a short notes file with the spreadsheet references and my micro-benchmark traces.

Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.com

Attachments: sizing_notes.md
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>

Date: Wed, 6 Jun 2028 12:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Pecos commit proposal and next steps

Hi Susan —

Thanks for the quick answers and the sample payloads. Based on Ben's microbenching and your token profile, we've converged on two practical options to present to procurement: 

Option A — Pilot-first (lower near-term commit)
- Commit: 8 slabs (q4_0) for pilot phase (30–45 days).
- Canary plan: route 10% traffic to Dedicated, measure p95 and KV hit rate for 14 days; auto-roll back to hosted if p95 spikes > 20% over baseline.
- If measured traffic aligns with samples, automatic uplift to 10 slabs on go-live (30–45 day window).

Option B — Go-live hedge (higher initial commit)
- Commit: 10 slabs (q4_0) immediately.
- Rationale: covers peak concurrency and gives ~25–30% buffer for deployment churn and feature rollouts.

Cost/ops items we will include in the formal proposal: per-slab monthly commit price, burst policy for transient spikes, SLA terms for p95, and an ops playbook for cache warmups and rollouts. Ben will add the microbench traces and suggested safety math; Marissa will include the onboarding & runbook steps for your SREs. 

If you approve, we'll (1) share a formal DocuSign-ready proposal and (2) schedule a 30-min kickoff with engineering (suggesting Thu Jun 8, 10:00 PT).

Attached: pecos_commit_proposal.pdf

Jordan Blake
